projects.name: TRC Search Widget
projects.tagline: Instant autocomplete across 139,714 Theodore Roosevelt Center archival items, in one script tag.
description: The Theodore Roosevelt Center's digital library indexes its holdings with a controlled Library of Congress vocabulary and no autocomplete, so a visitor who types “henry cabot lodge” gets nothing back. This widget fixes that from the outside.

A weekly job harvests the Center's public taxonomies, caches them as static JSON on GitHub Pages, and serves three drop-in web components off that index. Because the vocabulary is precomputed, suggestions appear as fast as the visitor types — and the archive's own servers never sit in the critical path.
Any institution whose collection search runs on a controlled vocabulary has this same problem. Point the harvester at a different WordPress REST API and the whole thing works for a different archive.
capabilities: <trc-search> autocomplete with live result counts, 6.9 KB gzipped
<trc-graph> interactive network map of 1,592 people or 1,600 subjects
<trc-topic> subject breakdown by format, deep-linked into the archive
Shadow-DOM isolation — host page CSS cannot reach in, widget styles cannot leak out
Every color exposed as a CSS custom property; three themes ship in the box
Weekly GitHub Action harvest with sanity checks that gate the deploy
setup: Fork the repo and point scripts/harvest.mjs at your own WordPress REST API host. It needs open taxonomy endpoints.
Run npm install, then npm run harvest and npm run head to build data/*.json for your collection. Add npm run fingerprints and npm run graphs if you want the relationship maps.
Add your palette to the shared token block in src/themes.js — a new institution is about a dozen lines — and set your accent and font defaults.
Replace CNAME with your subdomain, point DNS at GitHub Pages, and set the Pages source to GitHub Actions with Enforce HTTPS on.
Adjust the harvest cron in .github/workflows/, then embed with one script tag plus <trc-search>.

projects.name: TR Timeline
projects.tagline: A single-file timeline that sets one life against the history happening around it.
description: Roosevelt's milestones run above a central date axis; American and world events run below it. A visitor reading about the Badlands years sees, in the same glance, that the Statue of Liberty went up while he was there.

The embed code sets the window, so one file serves a full-life view or a tight six-year slice. Every date, label, and blurb lives in one plain data file — editing the timeline means editing data, never code. An expand icon opens a full-screen vertical version showing every point.
capabilities: Date-driven windows via data-start and data-end — year, month, or exact day
Named presets: full, earlylife, badlands, risetopower, presidency, postpresidency
Weight-based label density that re-fits itself on resize
Hover or tap for exact dates; click to pin an event in the readout
Full-screen vertical timeline with chapter dividers
Optional Explore buttons linking any point to a page on your own site
setup: Fork the repo. The whole widget is three files: tr-timeline.js, tr-data.js, and index.html.

Rewrite tr-data.js. It holds three lists — phases (chapter bars), events (your subject's milestones), and history (context events). Each entry takes a year, an optional exact date, a label, a weight from 1 to 5, and a blurb.
Swap the fonts and palette referenced in tr-timeline.js for your own, keeping the safe fallbacks.
Replace CNAME with your domain, or delete it to use the default *.github.io address. The deploy workflow publishes on every push to main.
Embed with <div data-tr-timeline data-start="1858" data-end="1919"></div> and one script tag. The widget finds its data file on its own.

projects.name: Family Tree
projects.tagline: Forty-six Roosevelts across six generations, every name opening a sourced biography.
description: Parents, siblings, both wives, six children, their spouses, and all seventeen grandchildren — with two lines carried down to present-day Library Trustees. Every person is a button; every button opens a biography drawn from published works in the Library's collection.

The layout is computed at runtime, so adding a person re-flows the tree instead of forcing anyone to bookkeep coordinates. Dates were checked independently against the Theodore Roosevelt Center, the National Park Service, and contemporary obituaries. That pass corrected two errors in the published books and surfaced a grandchild the sources never named.
capabilities: 46 people across six generations, laid out automatically
Biography dialog for every person, closing on Escape
Two published URLs — a branded standalone page and a bare embed.html for iframing
JavaScript API: mount(), open(id), fit(), home()
Shadow DOM isolation with graceful font fallbacks
CI renders the whole tree headlessly and refuses to deploy if nodes overlap
setup: Fork the repo. Everything published lives in site/.
Replace the PEOPLE and FAMILIES objects at the top of site/tr-family-tree.js with your own records. The layout re-flows when you add someone.
Rewrite the biography text in the same file, and document your sourcing in docs/SOURCES.md.
Swap the masthead and wordmark in site/index.html, committing your own SVG into site/ rather than hotlinking it.
Update site/CNAME and point DNS at GitHub Pages. The workflow verifies, then publishes on push to main.
Embed by iframing embed.html at an explicit height (700–820px), or drop the script into a page with <div id="tr-family-tree" data-height="780">.

projects.name: Photo Gallery
projects.tagline: Drop photos in a folder, run one script, embed a masonry gallery anywhere.
description: A build-and-embed pipeline for event photography. Full-resolution originals go into a folder; a Python script generates thumbnails, web-optimized lightbox images, and a manifest, all served from GitHub Pages. The host page needs two lines of HTML.

The numbers are the point: one gallery went from 926 MB of originals down to 5.6 MB of thumbnails plus 41 MB of images loaded only when someone opens the lightbox. Originals stay in the repo for archival purposes and are never served to a visitor.
capabilities: Masonry grid with lazy-loaded thumbnails and a full-screen lightbox
Idempotent build — only processes what has not been built yet
Multiple galleries on one page from a single script include
Namespaced CSS that will not collide with the host site
Configurable thumbnail width, maximum image side, and JPEG quality
No server, no database, no image CDN bill
setup: Fork the repo and delete the sample galleries from galleries/ and docs/galleries/.
Add your own folder of full-resolution photos at galleries/<your-name>/.
Run pip install Pillow then python3 build.py. Tune THUMB_WIDTH, WEB_MAX_SIDE, and quality at the top of build.py first if you need different sizes.
In Settings → Pages, choose Deploy from a branch, main, folder /docs.
Replace docs/CNAME with your domain, add the DNS record, and enable Enforce HTTPS.
Embed with <div data-gallery="your-name"></div> and one script tag pointing at your own embed.js.

projects.name: DAM Portal Embed
projects.tagline: Turns a locked-in press portal into native, auto-sizing gallery tiles on your own page.
description: Acquia DAM (Widen) portals can only be embedded as a fixed-height iframe with its own interior scrollbar, and the portal's JSON API sends no CORS headers, so a browser cannot read it directly. Both problems are solved server-side.

A scheduled job snapshots the portal's sections and galleries and permanently caches the thumbnails — necessary because Acquia's preview URLs are pre-signed and expire within a couple of hours. The result renders as ordinary page content that grows to fit. Clicking a tile opens the real gallery, deep-linked, so press users still download through Acquia's own controls.
capabilities: Native auto-sizing tile grid instead of a fixed-height iframe
Thumbnail caching that defeats expiring pre-signed URLs
Deep-linked lightbox into the real portal gallery and its download controls
Refresh every six hours by GitHub Action, plus a manual trigger
Works with any Acquia DAM portal — add it to config.json
About twenty data-* styling options: accent, fonts, tile size, aspect ratio, badges
setup: Fork the repo and replace the entry in config.json with your portal: domain, shortcode, and path. The path is the portal URL segment with spaces removed.
Commit, then run the update-portal-data Action manually. It writes data/<shortcode>.json and downloads thumbnails into data/thumbs/<shortcode>/.
Enable GitHub Pages and set your own CNAME and DNS if you want a custom domain.
Override the brand defaults on the script tag with data-accent, data-rule, data-heading-font, and data-title-font.
Paste the embed into any raw-HTML block, pointing data-data-url at your own generated JSON.

projects.name: Hours Embed
projects.tagline: Republishes hours locked inside one CMS as a live embed on a completely different site.
description: The Library's restaurant, Salt + Scoria, keeps its hours in Drupal on trlibrary.com, which blocks cross-origin requests. The restaurant's own Squarespace site therefore could not read them, and staff were updating two places by hand.

A scheduled job scrapes the hours markup and its schema.org JSON-LD every six hours and writes a small JSON file. GitHub Pages serves that file with permissive CORS, and a tiny embed renders seasonal tabs on the Squarespace page. If parsing ever breaks, the script exits non-zero and the last good file stays published — the page never goes blank.
capabilities: Six-hourly sync of seasonal tabs, service rows, and holiday closures
Fails safe — a broken parse never overwrites good published data
Detects the current season by date, with a year-agnostic fallback
Background-aware theming that flips to light-on-dark over colored sections
Adopts the host page's own heading and body fonts
Shadow DOM isolation from the host CMS's stylesheet
setup: Fork the repo and change the source URL in scripts/extract-hours.mjs to your own hours page.
Rewrite the parser's selectors to match your markup. Use --fixture test/fixture.html against a saved copy of your page to test offline.
Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch, main, folder /docs.
Settings → Actions → General → Workflow permissions → Read and write, so the sync job can commit its output.
Run the Sync hours workflow once by hand to publish live data.
Add a code block on the host site with <div data-trpl-hours></div> and your embed URL. Set data-theme and data-accent to match your brand.

projects.name: Ticketing Widgets
projects.tagline: Live sell-out warnings and best-day-to-visit advice, refreshed every fifteen minutes.
description: Six embeddable widgets that turn a ticketing system's reporting API into plain guidance for visitors: which timed-entry slots are gone, whether a day is likely to sell out, and which nearby days are a better bet.

A GitHub Action runs two reports every fifteen minutes and publishes static JSON. There is no server to run and no API key exposed in a browser. Risk is modeled as supply against expected weekday demand rather than raw percent sold, because a day sitting at 60% the night before can still sell out to walk-ups by mid-morning.
capabilities: Six widgets: alert banner, time-slot grid, week planner, date check, month outlook, year heatmap
Sitewide dismissible floating banner, deployable through Google Tag Manager
Sell-out risk model using sales pace, lead curves, and day-of-week behavior
Permanent monthly archive enabling year-over-year ghost overlays
Hand-maintained closures file honored by every widget, with named reasons
Staff-facing monitor page; mock mode runs the whole stack with no API key at all
setup: Ask your ticketing admin to create a reporting-only integration user and request an API key. Until it arrives the repo runs in mock mode and the whole demo works end to end.
Add ACME_API_KEY as a repository secret. Set the report-ID repository variables — the shipped defaults are the Library's own report definitions and must be replaced.
Edit closures.json with your holiday closures and weekly closed days per season, and set your thresholds and tickets URL in config.json.
Settings → Pages → Deploy from a branch, main, root. Replace CNAME and add the DNS record.
Run the Update availability data workflow, then check that the generated JSON looks right.
Add the script once per page plus any <div data-trpl-widget="…"> containers. Tune the thresholds in day_risk() if your demand pattern differs.

projects.name: Trip Planner
projects.tagline: A wizard that turns a guest's interests into a routed, dated, printable itinerary.
description: Ten questions about interests, dates, travel style, and lodging comfort produce an hour-by-hour itinerary the guest can print, share, or drop into a calendar. It is rule-based and deterministic — there is no model in the loop and nothing to hallucinate.

Everything it knows lives in plain JSON files, so editing the planner means editing data, not code. The scheduler routes distant stops as en-route legs with gateway-city overnights while holding the in-town stay in one contiguous block, so the guest books a single hotel instead of three.
capabilities: Ten-step wizard across 43 regional stops and a 60-plus item local catalog, filtered by season
Scheduler honoring opening hours, meal windows, one evening show per night, and pace budgets
Airport recommendation including open-jaw routing, validated against rental-car coverage at both ends
Shareable permalinks, calendar export, and a purpose-built print page
Fix-it-here controls that re-lay an over-full plan in real time
Two weekly jobs: a live event refresh and a link-rot watchdog that opens issues rather than editing data
WCAG 2.1 AA verified with axe-core — zero violations
setup: Fork the repo and read CLAUDE.md first — it is the builder's guide to the architecture, the scheduler rules, and the gotchas.

Rewrite the JSON in data/: origins, airports, destinations, lodging, your local catalog, your own venue and tours, weather, and itineraries. Each file carries a note field explaining its shape. Do not hand-edit the events file — it is generated.
Set your brand colors, comfort tiers, and travel styles in data/config.json.
Repoint scripts/refresh-events.mjs at your own event sources and update the monitored shows in the freshness checker.
Settings → Pages → Source = GitHub Actions. Set your CNAME and DNS, and set Workflow permissions to Read and write so the refresh can commit.
Add your own photos by setting each item's image to a URL and running the image-caching script.

projects.name: Local Weather
projects.tagline: Live local weather as a one-line embed, plus auto-refreshing forecast images for email.
description: A job pulls National Weather Service data and air-quality readings about every thirty minutes, normalizes them into a cached JSON file, and renders both a zero-dependency JavaScript widget and a set of static PNG and SVG forecast images.

Everything the public loads is a static file on a CDN, so visitor traffic never touches the government API and the rate limits never bite. The images are hotlinkable, which means a newsletter can show today's forecast without any JavaScript at all.
capabilities: One-tag widget with data-* options for days, hours, rain, view, and refresh interval
Five views: mini badge, current conditions, hourly, multi-day, alerts
Hotlinkable PNG and SVG images including a 1200×630 social card
Live severe-weather alert banners with severity tinting and five-minute polling
Feels-like, wind and gusts, humidity, sunrise and sunset, air quality, snowfall
Stale-data fallback: serves the last good forecast and flags it rather than going blank
setup: Fork the repo, then edit config.json and set location — name, region, latitude, longitude, timezone — to your own place.
In the same file set your base URL, custom domain, full-forecast link, and a real contact string for userAgent. The National Weather Service requires one.
Replace the brand colors, fonts, and icons in src/lib/brand.mjs and src/lib/icons.mjs, and swap the font files for ones you have web-embedding rights to.
Settings → Pages → Source = GitHub Actions. Add your DNS record, set the custom domain, and enable Enforce HTTPS.
Run npm install && npm run build locally to confirm, then push. The workflow takes over on its half-hourly schedule.

projects.name: Living Building Dashboard
projects.tagline: A lobby display turning building performance into a living Badlands panorama.
description: A single self-contained HTML file built for a widescreen lobby screen, showing energy, water, and air-quality performance against the seven petals of Living Building Challenge 4.0. The backdrop is a vector Badlands scene with a real day-night cycle and live local weather rendered as clouds, rain, snow, fog, or lightning.

Worth knowing before you fork it: this is a working prototype driven by browser-generated demo data. The next phase wires it to the Library's building management system. What it gives you today is the whole presentation layer and one clearly marked place to swap the data source.
capabilities: Overview screen with floating KPI tiles for energy, solar, geothermal, water, and CO₂
Seven-petal navigation rail with per-petal drill-in pages
Animated landscape: sun and moon arc, sky phases, stars, weather effects
Live local conditions with no API key required
A single adapter block designed as the one place to swap demo data for live data
Companion spreadsheet for the petals that are documented by hand
setup: Fork, replace CNAME with your hostname, set Settings → Pages → Source to GitHub Actions, and add the DNS record.
Edit index.html — swap the palette, the headline copy, and the petal narrative text for your own building's story.
Change the latitude and longitude in the weather call so the scene reflects your site, or remove the scene entirely.
Confirm your building management system actually meters what you want on screen. Anything unmetered belongs in the spreadsheet, not on the wall.
Replace tickDemo() inside the data-source block with a fetchLive() returning the same field names.
Never put an API token in index.html — it is public. Route through a proxy or a scheduled job that commits a static JSON file.

projects.name: Social Calendar
projects.tagline: A shareable, read-only calendar of scheduled social posts, rebuilt twice a day.
description: Pulls scheduled social messages from the Hootsuite API twice a day, writes a JSON snapshot plus downsized preview images, and publishes a dependency-free static site. One story going to six channels renders as a single row with per-network icons, not six near-identical duplicates.
A second page rebuilds a link-in-bio archive by following shortlinks to their real destinations and reading each page's own headline, so the archive outlives the calendar's two-week window.
One caution before you deploy it publicly: the published site exposes copy that has not gone out yet. Put access control in front of the hostname if that matters to your organization.
capabilities: Month grid and forward-running agenda views over the same snapshot
Per-network previews that mimic how copy will actually look once posted
Filter by channel, tag, and status; full-text search of post copy
Link-in-bio page with a merging archive
Timed reveal so scheduled posts appear on time without waiting for a rebuild
OAuth refresh-token rotation written back to a repository secret automatically
setup: Fork, replace CNAME, set Settings → Pages → Source to GitHub Actions, and add the DNS record.
Follow SETUP.md: register a developer app with your scheduling platform and add the three required repository secrets. About ten minutes, once.
Run scripts/bootstrap_auth.py once locally to complete the OAuth handshake and seed the refresh token.
Point the brand tokens at your own colors and fonts.
Adjust the cron in .github/workflows/refresh.yml if twice daily is not your cadence, then trigger it once with a backfill to seed the links archive.
Decide whether the site should be public. It shows unsent copy.

projects.name: Newsletter Builder
projects.tagline: A browser newsletter builder that exports paste-ready HTML for your email platform.
description: A block-based email builder that runs entirely in the browser with no backend. Assemble blocks, edit each one in a side panel, and export HTML ready to paste into Constant Contact's code-your-own editor — or any platform that accepts raw HTML.
A companion Header Studio composites a wordmark plaque over a photograph and hands back a branded PNG header, which removes the most common reason a staff member has to open a design tool at all.
capabilities: Block library plus a one-click standard template
Per-block editing with reorder, duplicate, and delete
Export HTML sized for a code-your-own email editor
Save an HTML file with the design data embedded, then reopen it to keep editing
Browser autosave of work in progress
Header Studio: photo upload, drag to reposition, plaque and wordmark color picking, PNG download
Ships with CLAUDE.md and llms.txt so an AI assistant can build newsletters in it directly
setup: Fork, replace CNAME, set Pages to deploy from main at the root, add the DNS record, and enable Enforce HTTPS.
Edit index.html to swap the colors, fonts, and default template block set for your organization's newsletter layout.
Replace the logo and wordmark art in assets/, used by both the builder and Header Studio.
Update header.html with your own plaque shape and brand color options.
No API keys are needed. Images still have to live in your email platform's library or DAM and be referenced by URL.

projects.name: Link Checker
projects.tagline: A weekly crawl that finds every broken link and typo across an entire website.
description: A scheduled job crawls a whole site from its sitemap, validates every internal and external link, spell-checks visible text against a dictionary plus an allow-list, and publishes an interactive report.

Issues are grouped by the page they appear on with links straight to what needs fixing, which is the difference between a report someone acts on and a CSV nobody opens. Two dismissal paths exist: a per-browser Ignore button for triage, and a shared committed ignore file for decisions the whole team should keep.
capabilities: Sitemap-seeded breadth-first crawl across every subdomain of one root domain
HEAD-then-GET validation that separates real breaks from bot-protection warnings
Spell check split into likely typos and unknown words, so names and jargon do not drown the signal
Interactive report grouped by page, plus machine-readable JSON
Per-browser Ignore that generates copy-ready lines for the shared ignore file
Threaded crawling and validation, tuned by environment variables
setup: Fork the repo and set Settings → Pages → Source to GitHub Actions. That is the only required manual step.
Set ROOT_DOMAIN to your domain and SITEMAP_URLS to your sitemaps in the workflow file.
Adjust the cron if Monday morning is not the cadence you want.
Seed custom_words.txt with your place names, donor surnames, and jargon so the first report is not swamped by false positives.
Test locally first with MAX_PAGES=25 python run_check.py and open the generated report.

projects.name: Reviews
projects.tagline: Collects visitor reviews daily, classifies the themes, and triages what needs a reply.
description: A daily job pulls reviews from Google, TripAdvisor, Yelp, and Facebook, merges them incrementally, classifies each one into a controlled theme vocabulary, and derives windows, deltas, theme movement, and a response queue for a static dashboard. There is no server and no database — every number on screen is also a line in git history.

A separate embeddable widget publishes vetted five-star pull quotes to the public website, guarded by three gates: a verbatim match against the original review, a regex screen, and an adversarial critic pass. The theme vocabulary grows on evidence rather than on a hunch, and new themes are re-applied to the full corpus so year-over-year comparisons stay honest.
capabilities: Multi-platform incremental collection with a periodic reach-back to catch new replies
Theme, sentiment, and tone classification with a deterministic keyword fallback
Self-growing theme vocabulary, promoted only on evidence and then re-applied to history
Response triage queue with SLAs, plus a hand-written executive brief
Rotating public quote widget in four layouts, with luminance-aware text color
Three-gate quote safety: verbatim match, regex screen, adversarial critic
Pre-commit validator that refuses to ship unparseable data
setup: Fork, replace CNAME, set Settings → Pages → Source to GitHub Actions, and add the DNS record.
Add the collection and model API keys as repository secrets. A local .env is invisible to Actions, so both places need them.
Edit config.json to point the sources block at your own listings, and set your SLAs and window sizes.
Verify the model path with the --check flag before trusting a full run.
Replace the theme vocabulary and review data with your own vocabulary and an empty dataset, then run a full backfill.
Before putting the quote widget on a public site, confirm each platform's terms permit excerpting review text.

projects.name: Anniversaries
projects.tagline: Shows which milestones hit a round anniversary this year and the next five.
description: A small static page that reads a curated list of dated events and surfaces those whose anniversary in a given year lands on a multiple of five. Tabs cover the current year plus five ahead, each entry showing the original date, the anniversary number, and a sentence or two of context.

It exists because commemoration planning happens a year out, not a week out. Any institution with a founder, a building, or a collection has the same problem — replace one JSON file and it is your chronology.
capabilities: Tabbed view across six years, current year first
Automatic five-year-multiple anniversary calculation
Month-and-day sorting, with undated entries falling to the bottom
The whole dataset editable as one plain JSON file, no build step
Deploys on every push to main
setup: Fork the repo and set Settings → Pages → Source to GitHub Actions.
Replace events.json with your own events. Each object takes a year, optional month and day, a title, and a description.
Swap the logo and edit the headings, colors, and copy in index.html.
Add a CNAME file and matching DNS record if you want a custom hostname.
Preview locally with python3 -m http.server 8000 — the page fetches its JSON, so a file:// URL will not work.
Verify every date against a primary source before publishing.

projects.name: Campus Map
projects.tagline: A 3D model of the campus you can spin, zoom, and pin with story markers.
description: A web viewer for a compressed 3D model of the Library campus. Visitors orbit and zoom the terrain and buildings, click a point of interest to open a panel with an image, text, and a call to action, and share the exact view they are looking at through a short link.

The engineering that makes it usable is the compression — 7.7 MB delivered from a 256 MB source — and the occlusion: markers hide themselves when a building or a berm stands between them and the camera, computed against a precomputed height map rather than GPU raycasting. A visual editor lets a non-developer right-click to place pins and download the resulting file.
capabilities: Draco-compressed, GPU-instanced campus model at 7.7 MB
Clickable markers opening an image, description, and call-to-action panel
Markers auto-hide when a building or berm blocks the line of sight
Shareable view tokens encoding camera angle, zoom, target, and open marker
Visual editor — right-click to place pins, download the JSON
One-line embed with per-embed custom marker sets
setup: Fork the repo, replace the GLB with your own Draco-compressed campus model, and regenerate heightfield.json for the new geometry.
Open /editor.html to right-click-place your own markers, then download and commit the resulting pois.json. Put marker photos in img/poi/.
Replace the wordmark in img/ and update the @font-face URLs in index.html — they point at fonts hosted on trlibrary.com and will not work for you.
Edit CNAME and add a DNS record pointing at GitHub Pages.
Enable Pages with source GitHub Actions. The workflow publishes on every push to main with no build step.

projects.name: StarGazer
projects.tagline: Hold your phone up to the sky and it names the stars above you.
description: An embeddable night-sky explorer that uses phone motion sensors to identify constellations, planets, and bright stars overhead, with drag-to-look on a desktop. It is built for dark-sky places: a dim palette, an extra-dimming slider, and a red-light mode that preserves night vision.

All of the astronomy is computed on the device, so a single script tag turns any page into a working planetarium with no API keys and no server. Planet positions land within 0.3 degrees of the JPL reference ephemeris.

One thing to read before forking: the Indigenous star knowledge included in the repo is drawn from published sources and every entry is labeled as awaiting tribal partner review. The README is explicit that it should not be reused as-is.
capabilities: About 5,000 stars to magnitude 6, all 88 constellations with lines, boundaries, and stories
Device-orientation sky pointing with compass-offset correction; drag and pinch on desktop
Sun, Moon phase, and Mercury through Neptune from Keplerian elements
85 constellation figures pinned to their stars by three-star affine fit
See-through mode showing the rear camera behind a transparent chart — never uploaded
Tonight panel with sunset, full dark, moonrise, and eclipses, plus a live aurora estimate
stack: Vanilla JS built from source by a Python build step
setup: Fork, install numpy, and run the two build scripts. The three built files are not committed — the deploy workflow produces them.
Set your own location defaults on the embed tag with data-lat, data-lon, and data-place.
Edit the plain JSON content files for constellation paragraphs, dated sky events, meteor showers, and figures. No widget code changes needed.
Replace the wordmark and the brand font and color references.
Move the deploy workflow into place, set Pages source to GitHub Actions, edit CNAME, and add the DNS record. Motion sensors require HTTPS, which Pages provides.
Do not reuse the Indigenous star-knowledge content without your own tribal partner review.

projects.name: Quiz Platform
projects.tagline: Drop a fifteen-question quiz into any page with two lines of HTML.
description: A dependency-free quiz engine that embeds into existing CMS pages rather than living on a site of its own. Each question gives immediate feedback plus a paragraph of real history and a link out; finishing yields a score, an achievement tier, and a downloadable badge.

It also supports asynchronous challenge-a-friend links and live two-player races. The challenge link encodes the identical run — score, deck, name, checksum — entirely in the URL, so nothing is stored server-side and there is no account to create. The whole quiz mounts in a shadow root, so a CMS theme cannot reach in and the quiz cannot leak out.
capabilities: Two-line embed that mounts in a shadow root
New quizzes added by dropping one JSON file in quizzes/ — no code changes
Per-run shuffling of questions and options, so answer positions are worthless
Challenge-a-friend links that encode the entire run in the URL
Live head-to-head play over WebRTC with timers and graceful fallback to solo
Gallery widget with search, difficulty and topic facets, and a daily reshuffle
Keyword search index built from proper nouns and rare words inside the questions
setup: Fork, then copy a sample quiz to quizzes/<your-id>.json and replace the content. Exactly 15 questions with 4 options each, a zero-based answer index, plus an explanation, image, credit, and link per question.
Put imagery in assets/img/<your-id>/ and fill in credits.json. Credit the source collection, never your DAM.
Add an entry to quizzes/index.json with difficulty and topics, then run the reindex script to rebuild the search keywords.
Replace the brand art and repoint the @font-face URLs in assets/css/trpl.css, which currently load from trlibrary.com.
Enable Pages from main at the root, edit CNAME, add the DNS record, and enforce HTTPS.
Point the embed snippet's script src at your own host and paste it into a full-HTML block on your CMS page.

projects.name: Rough Rider
projects.tagline: A ten-chapter 8-bit platformer that plays an entire life, mini-games and all.
description: Ten chapters carry Roosevelt from 1858 to 1919, each a platformer level over a painted backdrop, each ending in its own themed mini-game and then a study recap. Hidden treasure chests reveal forty real, sourced facts, and the recap tallies which the player found and which they missed.

It runs with no installation, no build step, and no network connection. The entire soundtrack is synthesized in the browser — there is not a single audio file in the repo. Finishing all ten chapters unlocks a promo code for a free youth admission, which is the part a museum actually cares about.
capabilities: Ten chapters, each with a cutscene, a platformer level, a unique mini-game, and a recap
Forty collectible history facts checked against the Library's book collection
Era-correct enemies per chapter, with the character visibly aging and changing costume
Fully synthesized chiptune score and sound effects — zero audio files
Touch controls that adapt per mini-game, with letterboxed fullscreen and add-to-home-screen
Completion reward with a promo code, plus score and progress saved locally
stack: Plain ES, no framework or bundler
projects.demoNote: Served over HTTP only — the custom domain is still waiting on its certificate, so this one is a link out rather than a live embed.

projects.name: Elkhorn Panoramas
projects.tagline: Seven 360-degree panoramas that let anyone stand inside the Elkhorn Ranch ruins.
description: The site of Roosevelt's Dakota ranch house, captured in seven equirectangular panoramas and served through a minimal drag-and-pinch viewer. The viewer libraries are vendored locally — no CDN, no build step, no API keys.

Be clear-eyed about what this is: a working proof of concept, not a finished visitor product. There are no captions, no hotspots, no navigation between panoramas, and no branding. What it does give you is the shortest possible path from a 360 camera to a shareable web experience, which is exactly the thing most institutions overestimate the difficulty of.
capabilities: Seven full-screen drag-and-pinch 360-degree panoramas
Viewer libraries vendored locally — no CDN dependency

Custom domain on GitHub Pages with a working certificate

projects.name: Digital Invitation
projects.tagline: Turns any invitation image into an envelope that opens, addressed by name.
description: A reusable embed plus a no-code builder that wraps invitation artwork in an animated envelope: it rises addressed to the guest, turns in 3D to show a brand seal, the flap opens, the card slides out, and an RSVP button appears. The guest's name comes from a query-string parameter, so a mail merge gives every recipient a hand-addressed envelope.

The builder is the part that makes it usable by a development office rather than a developer. Eight contrast-checked brand presets, a live readout, and a warning when the envelope liner is too close in tone to the background — which is the single failure that makes an opened envelope read as a hole in the page. It also emits a matching email template and a downloadable zip, so a staff member can hand a finished campaign to the web team without writing code.
capabilities: Envelope-opening animation with 3D flip, seal, perforated stamp, and postmark
Per-guest personalization from a ?name= parameter, with a configurable fallback
Visual builder with eight WCAG-AA-checked presets and a live contrast readout
auto ink colors that measure contrast and pick dark or light text themselves
Rich-text details panel that cleans Word and Google Docs paste into an allowlisted subset
Email template built from table cells so the guest's name stays live text when images are blocked
Download-everything zip and a share link encoding the whole build in under 1 kB
stack: Single vanilla JS file, no dependencies

Open your copy of the builder, set data-card-image to your invitation artwork (portrait 5:7 or 2:3) and data-rsvp-url to your RSVP page, then copy the snippet.
Set data-font-kit-url to your own web font kit. Licensed brand faces cannot be bundled in a public repo, and without a kit the embed falls back silently to open substitutes.
Replace the branded art — the seal and wordmark in assets/, and the flattened PNGs in assets/email/. The emailed stamp is a flat PNG and ignores builder color changes.
Recolor with envelope-color, liner-color, accent-color, and background-color. Keep the liner perceptually distinct from both the background and the envelope paper.
Edit the email template, paste the builder's output into your platform's custom-code editor, and send yourself a test to confirm the personalization survives click-tracking rewrites.

projects.name: Got Two Hours?
projects.tagline: Tell it how much time you have, and it builds a route through the national park.
description: A visitor picks how much time they have and where they are starting — the Library, either unit of Theodore Roosevelt National Park, or the interstate — and the planner builds a route. By default it starts with the full Library visit, checks live timed-entry availability for the first open slot, then fills the remaining park time with stops drawn from the National Park Service's own "things to do" and places data.

The route engine scores each stop against the time it adds, swaps in better stops when they fit, and orders them by the shortest drive. It respects visitor center hours, sunset, and any NPS alert that closes a stop, and it never shortens the Library visit to make a plan look complete. The finished plan lives in the page address, so a staff member can send a guest a link to the exact day.
capabilities: Plans from 90 minutes to a full day, from four starting points
Live timed-entry check against the ticketing feed, with next-day fallbacks
Honors visitor center hours, sunset, and NPS closure alerts automatically
Drive times from OSRM over OpenStreetMap roads, with a cushion
"Roosevelt day" alternative that adds the Elkhorn Ranch on long plans
Shareable plan links, with UTM-tagged ticket links for GA4
Renders straight into the host page, no iframe, with scoped tp- styles
setup: Fork the repo and get a free NPS API key. Add it as the Actions secret NPS_API_KEY — the shared DEMO_KEY is rate-limited and will miss runs.
Edit data/stops.json for your park: NPS ids, minutes at each stop, a 1–10 score, and your own institution's visit length under library.visitMinutes.
Run node scripts/build-matrix.mjs and node scripts/build-nps.mjs to rebuild the drive-time matrix and park data.
Point the availability URL at your own ticketing feed, or turn the "start with" visit off with lib=0.
Copy docs/refresh-nps.yml into .github/workflows/, give workflows read and write permission, and enable Pages from main with your own CNAME.

projects.name: Wildlife Watch
projects.tagline: A field guide to the park's bison, wild horses, and twenty other animals, with recent sightings.
description: A guide to watching wildlife in Theodore Roosevelt National Park: a field guide to 22 animals, a full section on the park's wild horses, a map of where to look, an outing planner with sunrise and dawn windows for any date, and a roll-up of recent public sightings from iNaturalist.

The sightings are handled with care for the animals. No exact locations are published: reports are rolled up to named areas or one-kilometer squares, the newest two days are held back, and obscured records are skipped. Month-by-month charts are adjusted for how many people report anything at all, so summer crowds do not make every animal look like a summer animal.
capabilities: Field guide to 22 species with seasons, where to look, and charts of when each is reported
Wild horses section: history timeline, how bands work, and a coat-color guide
Map of viewing spots, sighting squares, and USGS bison range from GPS collars

Daily iNaturalist refresh with location privacy guardrails built into the build script
Printable family checklist and the NPS 25-yard rule
Seven embeddable views, each a self-sizing widget

Replace or remove the horse section in data/horses.json, and swap photos in assets/photos/ with their credits in credits.json.
Point scripts/build-inat.mjs at your own iNaturalist place id. Keep the location roll-up and the two-day delay — they protect the animals.

projects.name: Elkhorn Ranch Walking Guide
projects.tagline: A GPS and compass guide to Roosevelt's ranch site that keeps working with no signal.
description: A mobile walking guide to the Elkhorn Ranch site in Theodore Roosevelt National Park. A live map and compass lead visitors to each of the eight National Park Service tour stops along the path, and arriving at a stop opens its story in the words of Roosevelt and his ranch partner Bill Sewall.

There is no cell service at the ranch, so the guide is built to be saved before the drive: the app, photos, an aerial image, and topo tiles for both the trail and the road in. It explains the location and compass prompts before the phone asks, walks visitors through fixing blocked permissions on every common browser, and notices when a phone is only sharing approximate location.

Compass on Android and iPhone, with a GPS-course fallback while walking
Full offline mode through a service worker: about 3 MB plus topo tiles

Staff preview mode with ?sim=1 to walk the route from anywhere

Replace the stop coordinates and route line, and the aerial image in map/. NAIP imagery from USGS is public domain for any U.S. site.
Adjust the arrival radius and the far-away distance in app.js for your trail.
Update the offline tile ranges and the cache list in sw.js, then bump the cache version.
Enable Pages from main at the root, edit CNAME, and replace the icons and manifest.webmanifest with your own.

projects.name: Camping on Public Land
projects.tagline: Answers "can I camp here?" from a phone's location across a patchwork of public and private land.
description: The land around Medora is a patchwork of national grassland, national park, state trust land, wildlife areas, and private ranches, often with no fence between them and different rules on each. This tool answers one question from a phone's location — who manages this ground, can I camp here, and can I have a fire today — without the location ever leaving the device.

Around that button sit a map of public land by manager, today's fire restrictions and fire danger, rain on clay roads, permit and reservation links, and an offline map that can be saved before heading out. Land records rebuild weekly and conditions every six hours. When in doubt it says "check first," never "allowed."
capabilities: One-tap land check: manager, camping rules, and today's campfire status
Warnings near boundaries and when the GPS fix is poor
Quarter-mile no-camping zones around developed Forest Service sites
Campfire logic from county and agency declarations, fire danger, and Red Flag Warnings
Live check of electronically posted private land, requesting only the posted flag
Offline map that saves about five miles of topo around the map center
Opens a GitHub issue when the posted Forest Service orders change

Rewrite the rules in CLASSES at the top of docs/camping.js for your land managers, with a source for each.
Point collector/conditions.py at your state's fire danger and burn-restriction services and your forest's alerts page.
Never request owner or lessee fields from parcel services. The collectors here deliberately ask only for tract, access, and posted status.

projects.name: Hunting and Fishing Guide
projects.tagline: Can I hunt here, what's open today, and where to fish — from a phone, offline.
description: A companion to the camping tool for hunters and anglers around Medora. One button reads the phone's location and says who manages the ground, whether it is open to hunting, which hunting units it falls in, and legal shooting hours for that exact spot that day. On private land it asks the state whether the parcel is electronically posted.

Season dates are read from the state's proclamations every day, so next year's dates appear on their own; when a date changes or a season cannot be found, the workflow opens a GitHub issue. The regulation pages behind the written land rules are fingerprinted twice a week for the same reason. About 30 fishing waters are listed with species, ramps, recent stocking, and invasive-species notes.
capabilities: Land check with hunting units for deer, elk, pronghorn, bighorn, turkey, and lion
Shooting hours by spot and date using the NOAA solar method, with time-zone boundaries
Daily season-date parsing from state proclamations, with issues opened on change
Where-to-fish list filterable by species, with ramps, piers, and stocking history
Map with public land, walk-in tracts, no-shooting rings, posted land, and unit lines
Licenses, vendors, hunter education, and carcass rules in one view
Offline map that keeps land records, units, and shooting hours working with no signal

Rewrite build() in collector/seasons.py for your state's proclamation pages, and the land rules in CLASSES in docs/huntfish.js.
List your regulation pages in collector/check_sources.py so changes open an issue for a person to review.

projects.name: Lodging Finder
projects.tagline: Shows which hotels, cabins, rentals, and campgrounds near a small town are open for a visitor's dates.
description: Medora has a short list of places to stay, and they fill. This widget gives every hotel, cabin, vacation rental, and campground nearby its own card — photo, a one-line description, and one button — grouped by whether it is open for the visitor's dates, needs a direct check, or is full. Tabs split Medora, vacation rentals, nearby towns, and Dickinson.

A daily collector checks each source on a rotation that spends lookups where they matter: the next few weeks daily, the rest of the year weekly. Rates are discarded and never shown. Staff get a monitor page with every tracked night against every property, and a log of nights opening up and selling out.

Dated booking links, so the button opens the right site on the right dates

projects.name: Today in the Badlands
projects.tagline: One strip with today's park alerts, weather, river, air quality, and things to do.
description: An embeddable strip with what a visitor needs to know this morning: park closures and road events, National Weather Service alerts, current weather, the Little Missouri River against its normal range, modeled air quality with smoke flagged, sunset and moon phase, and the park's activities filtered by how much time the visitor has.

An hourly build pulls every source into one snapshot and keeps the last good value, flagged, when a source fails. In the browser, weather, alerts, river, and air are then refreshed live every fifteen minutes. Activities with no official duration are grouped under "at your own pace" rather than given made-up times.

projects.name: Northern Lights Watch
projects.tagline: Tonight's aurora outlook, a year-ahead trip planner, and what records since 1932 say about when to come.
description: An embeddable northern lights outlook for one place. For tonight and the next two nights it combines NOAA's space-weather forecast with cloud cover and moonlight after dark and gives a plain rating, from "unlikely" to "strong." When it is dark and activity is up, it reads NOAA's 30-minute aurora model for the sky to the north and says so.

The trip planner scores every night of the coming year from what the record says: seasonal odds since 1940 of aurora-strength activity under a mostly clear sky, where the solar cycle stands, moonlight, and NOAA's 45-day outlook where it reaches. It lists the five best three-night stretches and links straight to lodging on those dates.
capabilities: Three-night outlook from NOAA Kp forecast, cloud cover, darkness, and moon
"Active now" note from NOAA's OVATION model when warranted
Year-ahead planner ranking every night, with the five best three-night windows
Nightly record since 1932 built from GFZ Kp and ERA5 cloud cover
Compact, planner-only, and full views for different pages
Lodging links that pass check-in date and nights to a lodging finder
Single-file, dependency-free, shadow-DOM widget

projects.name: Giving Tools
projects.tagline: Sixteen planned-giving calculators and guides, each one script tag, with nothing a donor types leaving the page.
description: A set of self-contained embeds for planned and tax-smart giving: a six-question Giving Navigator that ranks options with reasons, an IRA charitable rollover calculator, a stock gift comparison, a bunching comparison, a state-by-state chart, bequest and beneficiary guides, an estate tax estimator, life-income illustrations, and more. projects.name: How the Library Works
projects.tagline: A 3D cutaway of the building's geothermal, water, and carbon systems, traced from the construction drawings.
description: An interactive 3D model of the Library's energy, water, and carbon systems, built to explain its pursuit of Living Building Challenge certification. The site is modeled as a cutaway block of the butte, and each stop opens the ground or the building: all 216 geothermal boreholes, the mechanical room, the wastewater treatment train and leach field, the prairie roof assembly, and the solar canopies.

The geometry is not illustrative guesswork. Borehole positions, pipe routes, tanks, and equipment were vector-extracted from the conformed drawing set and registered to the campus model by matching building outlines, and terrain comes from USGS elevation data. Where a position is approximate or a part is drawn larger so it reads at site scale, the page says so.

Cutaways into the bore field, mechanical room, process tanks, and leach field
Exploded samples of the roof assembly and radiant slab

projects.name: Read the Rocks
projects.tagline: Tap anywhere in the park to learn which rock layer you're standing on and how it formed.

Tap anywhere on the colored geologic map, or follow your own location, and a card names the rock layer, its age, a plain-language story, and what to look for. projects.name: The Little Missouri
projects.tagline: Today's river at Medora beside the river Roosevelt knew, with a century of gauge records.
description: A river page in two halves. Today's River shows live flow and gauge height at Medora against every year on record for the date, paddling status from the park's own thresholds, flood stages, weather, alerts, and a 30-day chart against the normal range. Then & Now sets Roosevelt's own words about the river beside what the gauges have measured since, in eight chapters from 1805 to today.

The Maps section swipes or fades between historic layers — General Land Office survey plats, 1939 and 1957 aerials, 1970s topo — and today's imagery. The Record shows exactly which years exist at each gauge, every yearly peak, and lets a visitor lay any past year over this one. The page is honest that Roosevelt's own years have no measurements.

projects.name: The Bad Lands Cow Boy
projects.tagline: Every surviving issue of Medora's 1880s newspaper, transcribed and indexed day by day.
description: The Bad Lands Cow Boy was Medora's newspaper from 1884 to 1886, the years Roosevelt ranched here. This site puts every surviving issue online, transcribed and indexed: what the paper reported for any calendar week, a timeline of more than 4,000 dated events, every item that names Roosevelt, full-text search of about half a million words, and a gallery of nearly 200 period ads and cattle brands.

A people index matches more than 1,800 names across the paper's spellings, with short bios written only from the paper's own items and fact-checked against the full text. Timeline of dated events, filterable by month, topic, and person

projects.name: Who Owned the Badlands?
projects.tagline: Watch land around Medora pass into private hands, patent by patent, from 1889 to 1957.
description: A map of federal land patents in twelve townships around Medora, built from the General Land Office records. A year slider starting in 1883, the year Roosevelt first came to the Badlands, adds each parcel as its patent is granted, so a visitor can watch the homesteading boom and the federal buy-backs of the 1930s play out across the landscape.

Tapping a spot, or using the "What land am I on?" button, shows every patent for that ground with a link to the original record, today's land status, and the Native history of the area. A search answers "Did your family homestead near Medora?" and a set of story cards follows parcels that were patented twice.

Patent cards linking to BLM GLO Records, with today's land status

projects.name: Day by Day
projects.tagline: All 21,986 days of Roosevelt's life as an open dataset, a JSON API, and an explorer.
description: Every day of Theodore Roosevelt's life, from his birth in 1858 to his death in 1919, as a structured dataset. Each day carries a headline and summary, where he was, the people and places involved, letters to and from him, related archive items, and life-period tags. There are more than 4,700 people and 2,800 places in linked registries, and more than 127,000 Theodore Roosevelt Center digital library items attached to the days they belong to.

The facts come from a published chronology that is under copyright, so none of its text is reproduced: every summary was written fresh, and an automated check rejects any six-word run copied from the source. Each day cites the source's volume and page. Roosevelt's own words are included but flagged unverified until checked against the original.
capabilities: Static JSON API, rebuilt by GitHub Actions on every push
Explorer site and embeddable widgets
Linked people and places registries, most places with coordinates
7,358 letters with correspondent and topic, many linked to the letter itself
Thirty editorial life periods across four facets
Copy-check that rejects six-word runs from the copyrighted source
Data under CC BY 4.0 in JSONL and CSV
setup: Use the API directly: start at /api/v1/index.json. The data is CC BY 4.0; credit the Library.
To build your own figure's chronology, fork the repo and follow docs/methods.md and docs/schema.md.
Write day records into data/enrich/*.jsonl and keep the copy-check if your source is under copyright.
Run python pipeline/build_dataset.py and python pipeline/build_api.py.
Enable Pages through GitHub Actions; the workflow builds site/api on every push.

projects.name: Executive Orders and Proclamations
projects.tagline: Every executive order and proclamation Roosevelt signed, with texts, stories, and what each led to.
description: Every executive order and proclamation Theodore Roosevelt signed as president — more than 1,500 documents — as an open dataset with a static JSON API, an explorer, and embeddable widgets. Each record has a plain-language summary, categories, places, states, citations to the Statutes at Large and the American Presidency Project, and a text where one exists.

More than 500 documents carry sourced notes on reception, political impact, and legacy, and nearly 200 present-day parks, forests, refuges, and other places are traced to the document that began them on a Then and Now page. Every text is labeled by how it was checked: collated word for word against a primary printing, or a working copy from a digitization or volunteer transcription.
capabilities: 1,111 executive orders and 410 proclamations, reconciled across four source lists
Static JSON API and CSV, rebuilt on every push
114 public stories written from verified research entries
Then and Now: present-day places traced to the documents that created them
Links between documents that modified or revoked one another
Verification status on every text, with page-image links
Embeddable widgets and cross-links to Day by Day
setup: Use the API directly: start at /api/v1/index.json. The data is CC BY 4.0; the source documents are public domain.
To build another president's set, fork the repo and replace the catalogs in sources/, following docs/methods.md.
Record every date or title correction with its source in data/corrections.json.
Run python pipeline/build_dataset.py and python pipeline/build_api.py.
Enable Pages through GitHub Actions; the workflow builds site/api on every push.

projects.name: Pop-ups
projects.tagline: A self-hosted replacement for OptinMonster: a brand-locked builder that publishes through Google Tag Manager.
description: An in-house replacement for a pop-up subscription service. A five-step builder designs a banner, pop-up, slide-in, or full-window takeover in the brand system, previews it with the real runtime, and hands back code to paste into Google Tag Manager. One small runtime script decides which pop-up shows, where, and how often.

Publishing stays where it already is: only people who can publish the tag container can put a pop-up on the site, and the builder cannot change the live site. Pop-up settings are data, never code, and each carries a check value the runtime verifies. Email sign-ups go straight into Constant Contact, and every impression, click, and conversion lands in GA4.
capabilities: Five formats: top or bottom banner, pop-up, slide-in, and takeover
Guided builder that counts the pages a pop-up will appear on from the sitemap
Background photos with an automatic readability check and Canva templates
Embedded Constant Contact sign-up form styled to match
GA4 events with six custom dimensions, plus a JavaScript API
Debug, preview, and clear switches on any page URL
One-time GTM import that creates the loader, template, and event tags
setup: Fork the repo and update the site object at the top of popup.js: your fixed header, alert bar, and chat-button selectors, and the hostnames the runtime may run on.
Replace the brand looks in the builder and fonts.css with your own.
Import gtm/trpl-popup-setup.json into your GTM container (merge, rename conflicts) and register the six GA4 custom dimensions.
Point scripts/fetch_sitemap.py at your sitemap and move its workflow into .github/workflows/.
Enable Pages from main at the root and protect main — pushing to it changes the script every visitor runs.

projects.name: House File Stats
projects.tagline: A daily, privacy-safe dashboard of an email list's size, completeness, and growth in Constant Contact.
description: A dashboard of the email house file in Constant Contact: file size, how much of it is mailable, field completeness, per-source totals and sync freshness, public newsletter list sizes, a state and ZIP map, and growth over time. A collector pages through every contact each morning and keeps only counters.

Privacy is the design, not an afterthought. Contacts are held only in memory; the output is counts and percentages. Small ZIP codes are folded into state totals, internal list names stay off the page, and the workflow fails the run if anything resembling an email, phone number, or record ID appears in the output. Another organization can reuse it by editing one config file.
capabilities: Daily aggregate stats and a growth history committed as JSON
Field completeness with address fallbacks to custom fields
Per-source attribution, with "last record created" to show a sync is still landing
State and ZIP map with small-count suppression and masking
Privacy guard in the workflow that fails on personal data
Optional ZIP-to-state fixer, dry run by default
One config.yml holds everything account-specific
setup: Fork the repo and create a Constant Contact developer app with the contact_data and offline_access scopes.
Copy .env.example to .env, fill in the client id and secret, and run python authorize.py once for a refresh token.
Edit config.yml: title, source systems and how to recognize them, public lists, and address fallback fields.
Add the three secrets to Actions, enable Pages from main, folder /docs, and replace docs/CNAME.
Run the workflow once by hand. Keep the dashboard out of search engines; the included robots.txt and meta tags do that.

projects.name: Visitor Impact Dashboard
projects.tagline: Thirty regional feeds — park visits, airports, highways, lodging taxes, jobs — in one daily-updated tourism dashboard.
description: A dashboard that gathers the regional signals of visitation around the Library in one place: Library attendance and where ticket buyers come from, monthly visits to Theodore Roosevelt National Park and seven comparison parks, airport boardings, border crossings, interstate traffic counts near Medora, campground reservations, city sales and lodging tax payments, county tourism jobs, and visitor spending estimates.

Each feed has its own small fetcher, so when one public source is down the others still refresh, and a manifest records what was pulled when. Many of these sources were never meant to be scripted — scanned PDFs, rotated tables, WebForms pages, quarterly files of several hundred megabytes — and the repo documents how each one is read. Only aggregates are stored: no customer records, and survey respondent rows are discarded after weighting.
capabilities: About thirty independent fetchers across federal, state, and park sources
Daily GitHub Actions refresh that commits changed data and redeploys the page
Library attendance and visitor origin by state, distance band, and feeder metro
Control-park comparison that flags and excludes parks with counter outages
Town-level sales and lodging tax payments, with guidance on reading payment lags
Aggregates only: ticket counts per ZIP, never customer records
Every series published as CSV in data/
setup: Fork the repo and edit config/sources.json: your parks and comparison parks, airports, border ports, traffic counters, counties, and towns.
Run pip install -r requirements.txt, then the fetchers you need and python scripts/build.py. Each fetcher stands alone, so drop any that don't apply.
Replace the ticketing fetcher with your own system's, or remove it. Store only counts, never customer records.
Add the secrets and variables your sources need, such as a ticketing API key and BLS_CONTACT, an address the BLS will accept in its user agent.
Set Pages to deploy from GitHub Actions and give workflows read and write permission. The first DB1B run downloads about 4 GB; later runs fetch only new quarters.

projects.name: The 1884 Diary
projects.tagline: Turn the pages of Roosevelt's 1884 pocket diary, with a page-by-page transcription beside every scan.
description: Theodore Roosevelt's pocket diary for 1884, from the Library of Congress, as a book you can page through. Every one of the 410 scans is here, cropped to the page edge, with a page-curl reader, a transcription panel beside each page, an 1884 timeline, search across the entries, and deep zoom into the handwriting.

Each scan has one structured record, and every mark on the page is kept with whoever made it: the printer's dated headers and calendars, Roosevelt's own writing split into entries, tallies, tables, and lists, and later archival pencil marks kept separate. People, places, and animals are recorded as written, and any identification is marked uncertain unless the page settles it. A review workflow, curator's notes with draft and approved states, and a kiosk mode make it ready for a gallery as well as the web.
capabilities: Page-curl book reader with the transcription alongside each page
Deep zoom into every scan with OpenSeadragon
1884 timeline and full-text search across entries
Structured page records separating printed text, Roosevelt's hand, and later archival marks
Review workflow with a flagged-readings review file and per-page review status
Curator's notes with draft and approved states, and featured highlight pages
Kiosk mode with large touch targets, no outbound links, and an idle reset
No CDN dependencies: libraries are kept in vendor/
projects.demoNote: The transcription is still in review. Check any reading against the page scan before quoting it.
setup: Fork the repo and replace pages/ with your own diary or notebook scans, cropped and numbered in image order.
Write one record per scan in transcription/pages/<seq>.json, following transcription/SCHEMA.md and CONVENTIONS.md.
Run python3 tools/build.py to rebuild data/diary.json and the review file.
Review every reading against the scans, mark records reviewed, approve curator's notes, then set "showDrafts": false in data/config.json.
Enable Pages from main at the root and edit CNAME. Embed with ?embed, or run it in a gallery with ?kiosk.

projects.name: Scenic Loop Audio Tour
projects.tagline: A free GPS-guided driving tour of the park's South Unit loop, narrated by two hosts, that works offline.
description: A free driving audio tour of the South Unit Scenic Loop in Theodore Roosevelt National Park, hosted by two narrators, Nora and Wes. It starts at the visitor center in Medora, follows the drive around the loop in either direction, and plays each stop's clip early enough to finish as the car arrives. Stories fill the quiet stretches only when there is time to finish them before the next stop.

It is built for a phone on the dash with spotty service: it keeps the screen on, works fully offline once downloaded, and shows the next stop with its side of the road. Pull over and the side panel opens with on-foot details, quizzes, rock-layer diagrams, and real animal sounds. Crawl away from a bison jam and it asks what you are seeing and plays a short clip for that animal. A preview mode simulates the whole drive from home.
capabilities: GPS-triggered two-host narration timed to finish on arrival
Works in either direction around the loop, with side roads, U-turn and off-route detection
Full offline mode and screen wake lock for a dash mount
Speed gauge against posted limits, with a few gentle spoken nudges
Pull-off panel with quizzes, diagrams, photos, and animal sounds, shown only when stopped
Wildlife slowdown prompt that plays a clip for the animal you are seeing
Preview the drive from home with a simulated run, plus a script review page with sources
projects.demoNote: Beta. The tour is still being checked before public launch. Use preview mode to hear it away from the park.
setup: Fork the repo and rewrite script/tour-script.md: N: and W: for each host, Q: for a verbatim quotation with its source, src: for citations that are never read aloud.
Run python3 tools/lines.py to list the lines that need audio, voice them with a text-to-speech service you hold a public-use license for, and save each under audio-src/lines/.
Run python3 tools/assemble.py to build the clips, then tools/build_data.py with your route, stops, speed limits, and photos.
Drive it virtually with python3 tools/sim_test.py in both directions before anyone drives it for real.
Set Pages to deploy from GitHub Actions, add your CNAME, and let the park know before launch.
